analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare-based health plan on insurance exchanges and lifts the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices.
analysis.headline: The public-option and drug-negotiation bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the federal government offer its own health insurance plan, run like Medicare, on the marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act. Anyone who buys insurance on an exchange and isn't already on Medicare could enroll, starting in areas with little or no competition and expanding nationwide. Doctors and hospitals that take Medicare patients would automatically take the new plan's patients, paid at Medicare rates (with an optional 25% boost in rural areas), and the bill would remove the law's ban on the government negotiating prescription drug prices for Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on their own or through small employers, especially in areas where only one insurer sells plans or where premiums are high, would get a new lower-cost option backed by Medicare's provider network and payment rates. Medicare beneficiaries would benefit indirectly if the government could negotiate drug prices, which today it is barred from doing. People in rural and underserved areas would get an optional 25% payment bump for providers and priority rollout in their communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying their own health insurance

how_it_helps.text: The government would offer a 'Medicare Exchange health plan' on the ACA exchanges, starting in 2020 in rating areas with no more than one insurer or with provider shortages and high costs, and nationwide by 2023, with small-group availability in 2024 [S2][S3].

Providers enrolled in Medicare or a state Medicaid program would automatically be participating providers, reimbursed at Medicare fee-for-service rates, with the Secretary able to raise rural rates by up to 25% [S2][S3].

The bill strikes the statutory provision that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating prescription drug prices for Medicare, allowing negotiation that could be combined with negotiations over Medicare Part D drugs [S2][S3].

The plan would be a qualified health plan meeting all Affordable Care Act requirements, including essential health benefits, and premiums would have to cover the full actuarial cost of the plan rather than being subsidized by general revenue [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a new government competitor paying providers less, and brand-name drug makers would face a government empowered to negotiate prices. Taxpayers would fund a $1 billion startup reserve fund for 2018 plus unspecified technology funding. Doctors and hospitals would be paid Medicare rates—lower than typical commercial rates—rather than private-insurance rates, though they could earn more in rural areas.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $1 billion in 2018 to establish and administer the plan, plus unspecified sums for a data and technology fund [S3].

Because providers enrolled in Medicare would be required to participate in the new plan at Medicare rates—typically well below commercial rates—private plans could lose network access, and providers could see lower payments than they receive from commercial insurers [S3].

Premiums must cover the full actuarial and administrative cost of the plan, so savings would depend on Medicare's lower payment rates actually translating into cheaper premiums; the bill does not guarantee enrollees pay less than they do today [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give consumers in uncompetitive insurance markets a government-backed alternative priced off Medicare rates, and it would reopen the door to Medicare drug-price negotiation, which the 2003 law expressly prohibited. The main costs are the $1 billion startup appropriation and the hit to private insurers and drug makers; the main design risk is that forcing Medicare providers into the plan could squeeze provider revenue and shrink private networks. On balance it is a genuine consumer option, but its premiums are not guaranteed to undercut existing plans in areas that already have strong competition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet, joined by Sens. Tim Kaine and Dianne Feinstein, introduced the bill on October 17, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S3][S5].
Ten Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The action history shows no further action—no committee vote, no floor vote—after the initial referral, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: no government plan competed with them on the exchanges, and the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices stayed on the books. Consumers in markets with only one insurer were left without the new option.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare-X Choice Act, which would create a Medicare-based public plan on the exchanges and lift the Medicare drug-negotiation ban.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to the committee he chaired; no markup, hearing, or committee vote was ever held on it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill puts a government-run plan, priced off Medicare rates, on the same exchanges where they sell coverage—starting in the low-competition markets where they face the least competition. Insurers' interest in stopping it ran against consumers who lacked affordable options.

The bill strikes the provision that bars the government from negotiating Medicare drug prices, and drugs covered by the new plan would be paid at rates the Secretary negotiates. Drug makers benefit from the current prohibition, which ordinary people pay for in premiums and out-of-pocket costs.

Medicare and Medicaid providers would automatically participate in the new plan at Medicare rates, which are lower than commercial rates, but they would gain a guaranteed stream of paying patients—especially in rural areas, where rates could rise by up to 25%. Insurers in the same markets could lose network access to these providers.
